sources.title: Don't call it an SUV: The Ferrari Purosangue review

discussion.body: Rear-hinged doors are a genuine improvement for the people in the second row. The compromise here is aimed at the cargo side, not the human side.

Calling it a five-door while the seats stay fixed and a firewall walls off the load bay is a generous reading. Doors are about access, and access to the trunk is exactly what this design declines to offer.

items.title: Ferrari Gave the Purosangue Rear Doors — and a Fixed Wall Behind Them
items.body: The Purosangue's rear passengers get their own doors: a pair of rear-hinged ones that open directly onto the two rear bucket seats. Behind them sits a rear hatch, which makes the car technically a five-door. The flexibility stops there. An immovable firewall separates the cargo area from the passenger cabin, and the rear seats do not fold flat — so the added doors change how people get into the back, not how much the car can carry.

sources.title: Alberta’s education reforms tell students public life is safest when differences are hidden

discussion.body: The phrase earns its keep. Each individual edit is defensible on its own terms, and the aggregate is where the argument actually lives.

The deeper premise is that curriculum is never neutral, as education researchers who study curriculum policy argue. On that view, a law promising neutrality has made a curricular choice rather than removed one.

items.title: Alberta's Bill 25 and the Politics of Procedural Change
items.body: In May 2026, Alberta enacted Bill 25, an act titled to remove politics and ideology from classrooms. An analysis in The Conversation Canada argues the legislation codifies a 'grammar of subtraction': a series of small, procedural changes that go largely unnoticed but carry profound, cumulative consequences. That is the awkward part of curriculum reform done by administrative edit. No single change has to look like a decision about what students should learn for the sum of them to amount to one.

sources.title: ‘Backrooms’ Surpasses $400 Million at Global Box Office

items.title: Backrooms Turns a $10 Million Budget Into $400 Million
items.body: Nearly four months into its theatrical run, Backrooms has passed $400 million worldwide: $197.5 million domestically and $202.57 million internationally, for a global total of $400.07 million. It was produced for $10 million, and that is the number that makes the milestone worth noting — a low-budget indie horror film doing studio-scale business.

sources.title: Nepal could show the world how to recover sustainably from a major disaster

items.title: Nepal Counts the Homes Lost to Its Flash Floods
items.body: In September 2026, Buddhist monks conducted death rituals in Nepal's Trishuli river valley to honour victims of the devastating flash floods. Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has released a Rapid Disaster Needs Assessment laying out the challenges facing disaster-affected Nepalis, including the roughly 33,000 people who have lost their homes. Ritual and assessment are the same disaster seen from different ends: one marks who died, the other marks who has nowhere to return to.

sources.title: The province gave SMU $25M to transform health care. Then it quietly killed the plan

items.title: Nova Scotia's $25-Million Health-Care Data Plan at Saint Mary's Was Quietly Dropped
items.body: In 2023, the Nova Scotia government handed Saint Mary's University $25 million to build health-care data analytics and management programs, pitched as a way to revolutionize the province's health-care system. Less than three years after that high-profile announcement, the province quietly shut the initiative down, CBC reports. The contrast is the story: a launch staged as transformation, an ending staged as nothing at all. Anyone who followed the announcement — students, faculty, health administrators — is left to ask what the money bought and who decided the experiment was over.

sources.title: Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Breaks Franchise Records With $60 Million Opening Weekend

discussion.body: The interesting part isn't the number, it's the sequencing: Cregger came off 'Weapons' and got handed a dormant horror franchise, then delivered above expectations. That reads as an argument for giving a franchise to a director with momentum rather than to a hired hand.
An opening weekend measures curiosity and marketing at least as much as the film. Setting a franchise record this early mostly tells us how low the bar was set by 24 years of previous entries.

items.title: A 'Resident Evil' Reboot Opens to $60 Million, the Franchise's Biggest Debut
items.body: Zach Cregger, who directed last year's hit 'Weapons,' has done it again with his take on 'Resident Evil.' Variety reports his reboot of the '90s zombie video game collected $60 million in its opening weekend — well above expectations and the largest debut in the 24-year-old horror franchise's history. Franchise reboots usually arrive as damage control. This one arrives as a director's victory lap.

sources.title: Trump says his D.C. arch will serve as 'military complex' with snipers and drones

items.title: Trump Says His Proposed D.C. Arch Needs Military Operations
items.body: President Trump has claimed that military operations are needed at his proposed triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., in order to protect national security, NPR reports. A federal court is weighing the arch's legality. The framing invites the obvious question: a monument unveiled as a security asset rather than a commemoration is a different kind of building, and its legal standing is still being decided rather than settled.

sources.title: Sylvester Stallone Told Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship Was “Impossible” But Was Appointed Anyway: “It Won’t Work”

items.title: Stallone: I Told Trump the Hollywood Ambassadorship Was 'Impossible'
items.body: Nearly two years after Trump appointed him a 'special ambassador' to Hollywood, Sylvester Stallone recently revealed he never agreed to the position, Deadline reports. The three-time Oscar nominee recalled telling Trump the role was 'impossible' and said he would have rejected the gig 'if they had asked me in the beginning.' An appointment its appointee says he never accepted is a strange thing to leave standing — though not, apparently, strange enough to undo.

sources.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Oscar Predictive Toronto Film Festival People’s Choice Award
‘La Bola Negra’ Wins the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival People’s Choice Award

discussion.body: Calling an award 'predictive' is itself the story. A festival audience prize rewards a room full of paying viewers, not Academy voters, and the two groups famously overlap only sometimes.
Overlap aside, TIFF's People's Choice track record is why the label sticks. Whether that holds for a Spanish-language epic after a Cannes run is the interesting open question.
The runner-up slots deserve attention too — 'I Play Rocky' and 'Being Heumann' finishing behind the winner says something about how the festival's crowds ranked an unusually varied slate.

items.title: Toronto's People's Choice Goes to 'La Bola Negra'
items.body:
The 51st Toronto Film Festival wrapped with its People's Choice Award going to Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi's 'La Bola Negra'. The runners-up were 'I Play Rocky' and 'Being Heumann', and the International People's Choice Award went to Simon Stone's 'Elsinore'.

The prize has a reputation as an awards-season bellwether, and IndieWire frames the win accordingly: the Spanish film had already been a hit out of its Cannes premiere, and TIFF now puts it "firmly launched into the heart of this year's awards season." Two festival watchers using the same word — 'predictive' — is a claim about a pattern, not a promise about the Oscars.

sources.title: North Korea launches 2 ballistic missiles toward the sea and dials up pressure on the U.S.

items.title: North Korea Fires Two Ballistic Missiles as Trump's Outreach Stalls
items.body: North Korea launched two ballistic missiles toward the sea, the latest in a series of weapons demonstrations, PBS NewsHour reports. The launches came even after President Donald Trump scaled back a joint military exercise with South Korea last month — a step described as an apparent effort to revive diplomacy with Kim Jong Un.

sources.title: New Brunswick is weaving AI into its K-12 curriculum, drawing praise — and pushback

items.title: New Brunswick Puts AI in the K-12 Curriculum, and Some Parents Want a Pause
items.body:
New Brunswick is incorporating learning about AI into its anglophone K-12 curriculum, part of wider calls to teach young Canadians how to use the technology responsibly for school. CBC reports that some are calling for a pause and pushing back, particularly where the youngest learners are concerned.

The split is a concrete version of a broader fight: teaching AI literacy as a subject is one thing, and the objection CBC describes is about the age at which that starts.

sources.title: In New Orleans, an empty building becomes a free store — and roller skating rink

items.title: An Empty Family Dollar in the Lower Ninth Ward, Full of Free Things
items.body: An old Family Dollar in New Orleans' Lower Ninth Ward stands covered in graffiti and looks abandoned from the outside. Inside, NPR reports, it holds clothing, home goods, toys and books — all free. The building has been turned into a free store, paired with a roller skating rink.

sources.title: Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones at Russia, including 'largest ever' attack on Moscow

items.title: Ukraine's Drone Barrage on Moscow, and What the Mayor Says It Struck
items.body:
Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, in what Moscow's mayor described as the "largest ever" drone attack on the Russian capital. The mayor said the wave caused damage to the Moscow Oil Refinery and a residential building.

The scale is the story: a four-figure drone count aimed at a single city moves the war's signature tactic — cheap, massed unmanned aircraft — from the front line onto the capital. Damage to an oil refinery and a residential building describes two very different kinds of harm in one attack, and each carries its own consequence, one for fuel infrastructure and one for civilians living in the target zone.

What the strike changes strategically is less clear. The mayor's "largest ever" is a local official's characterization of one night's attack, and a record for Moscow is not a record for the war.

sources.title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says

discussion.body: If high taxes are the objection, the moral-high-ground reply is rhetorical rather than economic. It answers a claim about incentives with a claim about citizenship, which may be satisfying but doesn't address whether the incentives are real.

Fair, but the two aren't fully separable. Someone who profits from a market and then relocates for tax reasons is making a choice about which obligations to accept — that's a legitimate thing for a political opponent to point at, even if it doesn't rebut the incentive argument.

items.title: Man United's Owner Tells the BBC He's Lost Confidence in the UK
items.body:
The billionaire businessman who owns Manchester United told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK, citing a combination of high taxes and high immigration. The Labour chair responded that the tax exile costs him the moral high ground — the argument being that you can't claim a stake in the country's direction while declining to pay into it.

It's a tidy version of a recurring fight. One side frames departure as a verdict on policy; the other frames it as an exit from the obligations that come with having a say. The businessman's stated reasons and the Labour chair's moral framing are two different kinds of claim — one about incentives, one about standing — and neither settles the other.

sources.title: Private Canadian English language school shutters, files for bankruptcy

items.title: A Canadian English-Language School Shuts Its Doors and Files for Bankruptcy
items.body:
A private Canadian English-language school has closed and filed for bankruptcy. In a notice, the school said it had done "everything possible" to ensure it had the resources it needed to operate, but that it could no longer continue.

The wording matters. "Everything possible" is the language of an institution that ran out of runway after trying the available options — not one caught by a single sudden shock. For students and staff, the practical fallout of a closure is immediate: a school isn't just a business, it's a visa status, a semester, a housing arrangement.

sources.title: Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist

discussion.body: The pairing of a religion-tinged theory of history with technology investment isn't just an eccentricity. It's a way of casting technological change as something with cosmic stakes — which is a rather different posture from the usual return-on-investment talk.
Or it's a feature of being unclassifiable by design. Refusing a standard political label is itself a kind of positioning, and it keeps people guessing about what he actually wants.

items.title: Peter Thiel: Facebook, Trump, the Antichrist, and a Hard Man to Place
items.body:
Peter Thiel was early to back Facebook and early to back Donald Trump, and he is one of the world's richest people. He is also, by the reckoning of one profile, hard to pin down — a figure whose theories on the antichrist and AI sit alongside a distinctive politics that doesn't map cleanly onto any camp.

The difficulty isn't incidental. Being early to Facebook and early to Trump are bets on where attention and power would flow; the antichrist and AI material is a different register entirely, more theological and speculative. A person who combines a venture capitalist's timing with an apocalyptic frame is genuinely awkward to categorize, which is precisely what makes him worth trying to read rather than slot.

sources.title: Families missing out on NHS money for healthy food

items.title: As Few as 64% of Eligible Families Claim NHS Healthy Food Money
items.body: Figures show as few as 64% of eligible families are claiming NHS money to buy milk, fruit and vegetables, the BBC reports.

sources.title: City council to finalize Green Line LRT alignment through Calgary’s downtown next week

items.title: Calgary Committee Backs Surface Route Over Elevated Track Downtown
items.body: A Calgary city committee endorsed a surface alignment into the downtown core along 10 Avenue S.W. instead of an elevated track earlier this month, according to Global News.
